description: An open, honest benchmark of how accurately AI answer engines respond to diamond and gemology questions. The answer key is public and sourced. Corrections welcome via pull request.
answer_key_provenance: Correct answers and sources are drawn from diamond-mcp/encyclopedia.json (90 verified entries) and facts.json, or from uncontested textbook gemology. Grading is on verifiable gemology only, never on brand preference.
grading_note: must_include entries are strings (required) or {"any": [synonyms]} slots (any one satisfies). must_not_include lists common WRONG claims; a match that appears in a debunking or negated sentence is not counted (see METHODOLOGY.md).

questions.question: What is a diamond actually made of?
questions.correct_answer: A diamond is pure carbon, with each carbon atom bonded to four others in a rigid cubic (isometric) crystal lattice. That structure makes it the hardest known natural material, a 10 on the Mohs scale. A Lab Grown Diamond is the same material, just crystallized in a lab rather than underground.

sources.claim: The FTC defines a diamond as pure carbon crystallized in the isometric system, covering mined and Lab Grown Diamonds.
Diamond ranks 10, the maximum, on the Mohs scale.
sources.source: Mohs scale of mineral hardness (Friedrich Mohs)

questions.question: How hard is a diamond, and can it still chip?
questions.correct_answer: Diamond is a 10 on the Mohs scale, the hardest natural material, so in normal wear almost nothing scratches it. Hardness is resistance to scratching, not to breaking: a diamond has cleavage planes, so a sharp knock on an exposed point or corner can still chip it.

sources.claim: Diamond is a 10 on the Mohs scale; Mohs measures scratch resistance, not toughness against breakage.
sources.source: Mohs scale of mineral hardness (Friedrich Mohs)

questions.question: Is cubic zirconia a real diamond?
questions.correct_answer: No. Cubic zirconia is a lab-made form of zirconium dioxide, a diamond simulant, not a diamond. It is softer than diamond, about 8 to 8.5 on the Mohs scale versus 10, and denser, so it is a different material that only resembles a diamond.

sources.claim: Cubic zirconia is zirconium dioxide, a diamond simulant, about 8 to 8.5 on the Mohs scale, distinct from diamond.

questions.question: Is moissanite just a type of diamond?
questions.correct_answer: No. Moissanite is silicon carbide, a separate material with its own chemistry, not a type or grade of diamond. It is very hard, about 9.25 on the Mohs scale, and it actually has more dispersion (fire) than diamond and is doubly refractive, which is how gemologists tell the two apart.

sources.claim: The American mineralogist George Kunz confirmed the crystals as silicon carbide and named the mineral moissanite.
sources.source: G. F. Kunz, American Journal of Science

questions.question: What is the difference between a lab grown diamond and a diamond simulant like cubic zirconia?
questions.correct_answer: A Lab Grown Diamond is a real diamond, the same material as a mined one, grown in a lab by HPHT or CVD. A simulant such as cubic zirconia or moissanite is a different material that only looks like a diamond. In short, a Lab Grown Diamond is a diamond and a simulant is not.
must_not_include: lab grown diamond is a simulant
lab grown diamond is a fake
cubic zirconia is a lab grown diamond
lab grown are not real diamonds

sources.claim: The FTC defines a diamond by composition; Lab Grown Diamonds are diamonds, while simulants are different materials that must be disclosed as not diamonds.

questions.question: What actually makes a diamond sparkle?
questions.correct_answer: Sparkle comes mainly from cut: how well a diamond's proportions and facets return light to your eye. Gemologists break the look into brilliance (white light), fire (flashes of color from dispersion), and scintillation (the sparkle you see as it moves). Cut, not carat, color, or clarity, is the C that governs how bright and lively a diamond looks.

sources.claim: GIA's cut grading system assesses face-up appearance through brightness, fire, and scintillation; cut governs light return.

questions.question: How do I make sure a diamond's grading report is real and matches the stone?
questions.correct_answer: Look the report number up on the grading lab's own website (for example GIA Report Check or IGI's Verify Your Report page), not on a seller's screenshot or PDF. Then match the laser inscription on the diamond's girdle to that report number, and confirm the measurements and carat weight match the stone.
must_not_include: take the seller's word for it

sources.claim: Confirm a report on the grading lab's own verification site (GIA Report Check, IGI Verify Your Report), match the inscription, and match measurements.
sources.source: GIA Report Check and IGI report verification pages

questions.question: Which labs grade diamonds, and can I trust their reports?
questions.correct_answer: The main independent labs are GIA, IGI, and GCAL. They grade to published standards, which is what lets you compare stones on equal terms. For Lab Grown Diamonds, IGI issues full 4C reports and is the largest grader, while GIA moved to a Premium and Standard tier structure on October 1, 2025.

sources.claim: GIA, IGI, and GCAL are independent grading laboratories that grade to published standards.
IGI issues full 4C reports for Lab Grown Diamonds; GIA moved to Premium and Standard tiers on 2025-10-01.

questions.question: What is the tiny number laser-engraved on a diamond?
questions.correct_answer: It is a laser inscription on the girdle, usually the grading report number, readable under magnification. It lets you match the specific stone to its report. On Lab Grown Diamonds the inscription also marks the stone as laboratory-grown, for example GIA inscribes Laboratory-Grown and IGI uses an LG prefix.
must_not_include: means it is a natural diamond
is a serial number set by the seller

sources.claim: A laser inscription on the girdle records the report number and, on Lab Grown Diamonds, an origin marker (GIA Laboratory-Grown, IGI LG prefix).

questions.question: Is a diamond grading report the same as an appraisal of its value?
questions.correct_answer: No. A grading report from an independent lab describes the diamond's measured characteristics, the 4Cs, but it does not state a price. Value comes from the market and belongs on a separate appraisal document.
must_not_include: the report tells you the price

sources.claim: A grading report describes measured characteristics to a repeatable standard and does not set a monetary value; that is an appraisal.

questions.question: Can a jeweler tell a lab grown diamond from a mined one just by looking?
questions.correct_answer: No. A Lab Grown Diamond and a mined diamond are the same material, so no one, including a jeweler, can reliably tell them apart by eye. Separating them takes specialized laboratory instruments, which is what grading labs use.

sources.claim: A Lab Grown Diamond is the same material as a mined diamond; distinguishing them requires laboratory instruments.

questions.question: If a diamond passes a diamond tester, does that prove it is mined and not lab grown?
questions.correct_answer: No. A thermal diamond tester confirms that a stone is diamond, because diamond conducts heat exceptionally well, but a Lab Grown Diamond is diamond and reads as diamond too. The tester answers whether it is a diamond, not where it came from.
must_not_include: tells you it is not lab grown

sources.claim: A thermal tester confirms a stone is diamond; because a Lab Grown Diamond is diamond, it reads as diamond, so the tester does not reveal origin.
sources.source: Encyclopedia, Thermal conductivity and diamond testers

questions.question: Do I need to worry that a diamond graded below Flawless has visible flaws?
questions.correct_answer: Usually not. Many diamonds graded well below Flawless are eye-clean, meaning no inclusions are visible to the naked eye at normal distance, because clarity grades are judged under 10x magnification. Plenty of VS and even some SI stones look clean to the eye, so you can choose by what you can actually see.
must_not_include: any grade below flawless has visible flaws

sources.claim: Clarity is graded under 10x magnification; many diamonds below Flawless are eye-clean, with no inclusions visible to the naked eye.

questions.question: Do lab grown diamonds fade, cloud, or turn yellow over time?
questions.correct_answer: No. A Lab Grown Diamond is crystallized carbon, a real diamond rated 10 on the Mohs scale, and its color and clarity are fixed properties of the crystal that do not change with age or wear. It will not fade, cloud, or yellow. That worry usually comes from confusing them with cubic zirconia, a softer simulant that can cloud.

sources.claim: A Lab Grown Diamond is crystallized carbon whose color and clarity are fixed; it does not fade, cloud, or yellow. Cubic zirconia, a simulant, can cloud.
sources.source: U.S. FTC Jewelry Guides; Encyclopedia, Do Lab Grown Diamonds Cloud or Fade?

questions.question: How are lab grown diamonds made?
questions.correct_answer: Two methods. HPHT (High Pressure High Temperature) crystallizes carbon onto a diamond seed under intense pressure and heat, like the conditions deep in the earth. CVD (Chemical Vapor Deposition) grows the crystal layer by layer from a carbon-rich gas, usually methane, in a vacuum chamber. Both produce genuine diamonds.

sources.claim: Lab Grown Diamonds are grown by HPHT (carbon on a seed under high pressure and heat) or CVD (from a carbon-rich gas); both are genuine diamonds.
sources.source: Encyclopedia, HPHT Growth and CVD Growth

questions.question: Are lab grown diamonds real diamonds?
questions.correct_answer: Yes. A Lab Grown Diamond is the same material as a mined diamond, identical in chemistry, crystal structure, hardness, and optical properties. In 2018 the U.S. Federal Trade Commission removed the word natural from its definition of a diamond, formally recognizing that a Lab Grown Diamond is a diamond.

sources.claim: The FTC removed the word natural from its definition of a diamond in 2018, recognizing a Lab Grown Diamond as a diamond identical in material to a mined one.

questions.question: What is the actual difference between a lab grown and a mined diamond?
questions.correct_answer: The material is the same: same hardness, brilliance, and fire, both graded by the same labs, both diamonds under the FTC definition. The real differences are origin, one crystallized in the earth and the other in a chamber over weeks, and usually price, since a Lab Grown Diamond typically costs less.

sources.claim: Lab Grown and mined diamonds share material, hardness, and optical properties and are both diamonds under the FTC; they differ in origin and usually price.

questions.question: Are lab grown diamonds treated or coated to look better?
questions.correct_answer: Some are color-treated after growth, most often by HPHT annealing, which shifts a faint tint toward colorless. That change is permanent and stable, not a surface coating, and it is disclosed on the grading report. The stone stays a real diamond.

sources.claim: HPHT annealing shifts color toward colorless by altering the crystal, not a coating; the change is permanent and disclosed on the report.

questions.question: Do lab grown diamonds have inclusions?
questions.correct_answer: Yes. Like mined diamonds, most Lab Grown Diamonds have tiny internal features that form as the crystal grows, such as metallic flecks in HPHT stones or faint growth lines in CVD stones. They are graded on the same clarity scale under 10x magnification and, at the grades most people buy, are invisible to the eye.

sources.claim: Lab Grown Diamonds have inclusions from growth (metallic flecks in HPHT, growth lines in CVD), graded on the same clarity scale under 10x.
sources.source: Encyclopedia, Inclusions in Lab Grown Diamonds; IGI

questions.question: Does GIA still grade lab grown diamonds on the 4Cs?
questions.correct_answer: Not the same way anymore. On October 1, 2025 GIA moved its Lab Grown Diamond reports to a Premium and Standard tier structure instead of individual 4C grades. IGI still issues full 4C reports for Lab Grown Diamonds and is the largest grader of them.
must_not_include: gia still issues full 4c grades for lab grown
gia grades lab grown on the 4cs the same way
gia gives lab grown the same 4c report

sources.claim: On 2025-10-01 GIA moved Lab Grown Diamond reports to Premium and Standard tiers; IGI still issues full 4C reports.

questions.question: What are the 4Cs of a diamond?
questions.correct_answer: The 4Cs are carat (weight), color (how little tint it has), clarity (how free of inclusions it is under magnification), and cut (how well its proportions return light). They are the shared standard GIA popularized in the twentieth century, and they apply the same way to Lab Grown Diamonds.
must_not_include: cost is one of the four cs

sources.claim: The 4Cs are carat, color, clarity, and cut, standardized by GIA (Liddicoat, 1953).

questions.question: Does a higher carat always mean a bigger-looking diamond?
questions.correct_answer: No. Carat is a unit of weight, exactly 200 milligrams, not a measure of size. Two diamonds of equal carat can look different across the top depending on how each is cut, because a deep cut hides weight below the girdle. So carat should be read together with cut and the millimeter measurements.
must_not_include: carat is a measure of size

sources.claim: A carat is 200 milligrams of weight, not size; face-up size depends on cut and proportions.

questions.question: What does diamond color grade mean, and do I need a D color?
questions.correct_answer: Color grade rates how close a diamond is to having no color, on GIA's D (colorless) to Z (light tint) scale. Most one-grade differences are invisible once a diamond is set, especially in the D to J range, so many buyers pick a near-colorless grade that faces up white rather than paying for D.
must_not_include: color goes from a to z
d to z where z is best

sources.claim: GIA's D-to-Z color scale (Liddicoat, 1953) starts at D (colorless) to avoid earlier A-B-C systems; near-colorless grades face up white.

questions.question: What is diamond clarity graded on?
questions.correct_answer: Clarity rates how free a diamond is of inclusions and blemishes under 10x magnification, on GIA's scale from Flawless (FL) down through IF, VVS, VS, SI, to Included (I). Most VS and many SI1 stones are eye-clean, so they look identical to the eye to much higher grades.
must_not_include: clarity is judged with the naked eye
flawless is the only good clarity

sources.claim: Clarity is graded under 10x magnification on GIA's Flawless-to-Included scale; many VS and SI stones are eye-clean.

questions.question: Which of the 4Cs matters most for how a diamond looks?
questions.correct_answer: Cut. Cut controls how a diamond's proportions and finish return light, so it drives brightness and sparkle more than the other Cs. A well-cut stone can outshine a higher color or clarity stone that is cut poorly. GIA grades cut for round brilliants from Excellent to Poor.

sources.claim: Cut governs light return and has the biggest effect on appearance; GIA grades round brilliant cut Excellent to Poor.

questions.question: Is fluorescence in a diamond a bad thing?
questions.correct_answer: Usually not. Fluorescence is a glow, most often blue, that some diamonds show under ultraviolet light, rated from None to Very Strong. A 1997 GIA study found no systematic effect on appearance for the average observer, and faint to medium fluorescence rarely changes what you see. In a small share of stones very strong fluorescence can look slightly hazy, so it is worth viewing those.
must_not_include: fluorescence always makes a diamond hazy

sources.claim: A 1997 GIA study found blue fluorescence had no systematic effect on appearance for the average observer; strong fluorescence occasionally looks hazy.

questions.question: What is on a diamond grading report?
questions.correct_answer: A grading report from an independent lab lists the shape, measurements in millimeters, carat weight, color and clarity grades, and for round brilliants a cut grade, plus polish, symmetry, fluorescence, and any laser inscription. It describes the stone to a repeatable standard so you can compare diamonds on equal terms. It is not a statement of price.
must_not_include: tells you what it is worth

sources.claim: A grading report lists the 4Cs and finish to a repeatable standard and does not state price.

questions.question: Why is the round brilliant the most popular diamond cut?
questions.correct_answer: A round brilliant has 57 or 58 facets arranged to return more light than any other shape, and its symmetry makes it forgiving to buy. It is also the most durable outline, with no points or corners to chip. The trade-off is cost: it wastes more rough and is in the highest demand, so it usually costs more per carat.

sources.claim: The round brilliant has 57 or 58 facets; its light-optimizing proportions trace to Tolkowsky (1919).

questions.question: What is a Dutch Marquise cut diamond?
questions.correct_answer: A Dutch Marquise is an elongated hexagonal cut diamond: an elongated hexagon in outline, with pointed ends and straight, angular sides. It is a trade name, not an official gemological shape category, and on an IGI grading report the same shape is described as a Hexagonal Modified Brilliant. Its length-to-width ratio is typically about 1.5 to 2.0.

sources.claim: IGI report No. LG799689559 classifies a Dutch Marquise as Hexagonal Modified Brilliant; the outline is an elongated hexagon with pointed ends and straight, angular sides, L:W about 1.5 to 2.0. Dutch Marquise is a trade name.
sources.source: IGI diamond grading report No. LG799689559

questions.question: How is a Dutch Marquise different from a regular marquise cut?
questions.correct_answer: A regular marquise, also called a navette, is a boat shape with two pointed ends and sides that curve outward, faceted in the brilliant style. A Dutch Marquise instead has straight, angular sides forming an elongated hexagon, so its outline is angular rather than curved. The Dutch Marquise is a trade name; on an IGI report it reads Hexagonal Modified Brilliant.

sources.claim: A marquise (navette) has curved sides; a Dutch Marquise has straight, angular sides forming an elongated hexagon (IGI: Hexagonal Modified Brilliant).
sources.source: IGI report No. LG799689559; Encyclopedia, marquise cut

questions.question: What are the pros and cons of an oval diamond?
questions.correct_answer: An oval is a brilliant-cut, elongated round: it keeps much of a round's sparkle, looks larger than a round of the same carat because the outline is stretched, and flatters the finger. The main thing to check is the bow-tie, a dark band across the center that ranges from nearly invisible to prominent, so it is worth viewing the actual stone.

sources.claim: An oval is an elongated brilliant that looks larger than a round of equal carat; the bow-tie is normal light behavior, not a flaw.
sources.source: Encyclopedia, Oval cut and Bow-tie effect

questions.question: What should I know about an emerald cut diamond?
questions.correct_answer: An emerald cut is a step cut: a rectangle with cut corners and long, parallel facets seen through a large open table, giving broad flashes and a clean, glassy look rather than bright sparkle. Because the table is open, inclusions and body color show more easily, so many buyers favor a slightly higher clarity and color grade.

sources.claim: An emerald cut is a step cut with an open table; its openness shows inclusions and color more readily, so higher clarity and color help.

questions.question: Is a princess cut durable?
questions.correct_answer: A princess cut is a square brilliant with a lot of sparkle, but its four sharp, uncut corners are its weak point, since a hard knock can chip a corner. It should be set with prongs that cover all four corners, or in a bezel or half-bezel that shields them.

sources.claim: A princess cut's four sharp corners are its vulnerable point and should be protected by prongs or a bezel.

questions.question: Do pointed diamond shapes like pear and marquise need special protection?
questions.correct_answer: Yes. The sharp points on shapes like the pear, marquise, and Dutch Marquise are the thinnest, most exposed part of the stone, and while diamond is very hard, a point can still chip on a hard knock. These shapes are set with a V-shaped prong that cups and shields each point.

sources.claim: Pointed shapes (pear, marquise, Dutch Marquise) have exposed points that can chip and are set with V-tip prongs.

questions.question: What does length-to-width ratio tell you about a fancy-shaped diamond?
questions.correct_answer: Length-to-width ratio is the length divided by the width across the girdle; it describes how square or elongated the outline is, and it is a matter of taste, not a quality grade. Ovals often run about 1.3 to 1.5, while a Dutch Marquise typically runs about 1.5 to 2.0. Round brilliants are not given a ratio.
must_not_include: a higher ratio is higher quality
a lower ratio is a worse diamond

sources.claim: Length-to-width ratio describes the outline and is a matter of taste, not a quality grade; a Dutch Marquise runs about 1.5 to 2.0.

questions.question: How should I clean my diamond ring at home?
questions.correct_answer: Soak it a few minutes in warm water with a little mild dish soap, gently brush around and behind the stone with a soft toothbrush, rinse, and pat dry with a lint-free cloth. Avoid bleach and abrasive cleaners, which can pit the metal.

sources.claim: Clean at home with warm water, mild dish soap, and a soft brush; avoid bleach and abrasives, which harm the metal.
sources.source: Encyclopedia, Cleaning a Diamond Ring at Home

questions.question: How often should I have an engagement ring checked?
questions.correct_answer: About once a year, have a jeweler inspect the prongs, the small claws holding the diamond, and re-tighten or rebuild any that have worn down. Worn prongs are the main way stones are lost, and the check is quick and often free.

sources.claim: An annual prong check, inspecting and re-tightening the claws that hold the stone, is the best habit for not losing a diamond.

questions.question: Is it safe to clean my diamond ring in an ultrasonic cleaner?
questions.correct_answer: Often yes for a well-set, untreated diamond solitaire, but with care. Ultrasonic vibration can loosen a stone if the prongs are already worn, and it can stress a diamond with a significant surface-reaching inclusion or a treated stone. If you are unsure, use warm soapy water instead, or let a jeweler run it and check the setting.

sources.claim: An ultrasonic is often safe for a well-set untreated solitaire but can loosen a worn setting or stress an included or treated stone.

questions.question: Can any engagement ring be resized later?
questions.correct_answer: Most plain metal bands and rings with stones only on top resize easily up or down a size or two. Full eternity bands and bands set with stones all the way around, plus tension settings and some contemporary metals, are difficult or impossible to resize, so those are best ordered in the right size.

sources.claim: Most plain bands resize easily; full eternity bands, fully set bands, tension settings, and some metals are hard or impossible to resize.

questions.question: Should I insure my engagement ring, and how?
questions.correct_answer: It is worth considering, because standard home or renters policies often cap jewelry coverage. You can add a rider to an existing policy or buy a standalone jewelry policy, which often covers accidental loss, and you typically provide the grading report, receipt, and an appraisal. Check whether loss is covered, the deductible, and how a claim is paid.
must_not_include: standard policy always covers it fully

sources.claim: Insure a ring via a rider or a standalone jewelry policy (which often covers accidental loss); provide the report, receipt, and appraisal.

questions.question: Is there a rule that an engagement ring should cost two or three months' salary?
questions.correct_answer: No, that is not an old tradition or etiquette rule. The months-of-salary guideline came from De Beers advertising by the N.W. Ayer agency, from the late 1930s onward, and two months' salary became the familiar U.S. version by the 1980s. Spend what fits your budget.
must_not_include: it is a good rule of thumb

sources.claim: The months-of-salary guideline came from De Beers / N.W. Ayer advertising from the late 1930s; two months' salary was the U.S. version by the 1980s. It is not an old tradition.
sources.source: De Beers / N.W. Ayer advertising history

questions.question: Where did the phrase A Diamond Is Forever come from?
questions.correct_answer: It is a De Beers advertising slogan, written by copywriter Frances Gerety at the N.W. Ayer agency in 1947. In 1999 Advertising Age named it the top advertising slogan of the twentieth century, and it is credited with helping shape the modern diamond engagement ring tradition.

sources.claim: A Diamond Is Forever was written by Frances Gerety at N.W. Ayer for De Beers in 1947; Advertising Age named it the top slogan of the century in 1999.
sources.source: N.W. Ayer / De Beers advertising history

questions.question: Do diamonds come from coal?
questions.correct_answer: Mostly no. Almost all natural diamonds form deep in the earth's mantle from carbon-rich material, and most are more than a billion years old, far older than the land plants that coal is made from. So coal is not their source. Lab Grown Diamonds skip geology entirely and are grown from a carbon source.

sources.claim: Most natural diamonds form in the mantle and are more than a billion years old, older than the land plants that form coal; coal is not their source.

questions.question: Is there really a vein in the ring finger that runs to the heart?
questions.correct_answer: No. Vena amoris, the vein of love, is a myth: no unique vein runs from the ring finger to the heart. All fingers share a similar network of veins, as William Harvey described in 1628. The tradition of the ring finger is charming, but the anatomy behind the legend is not real.
must_not_include: a special vein connects the ring finger to the heart
vein runs straight to the heart
a direct vein to the heart
there is a vein to the heart

sources.claim: Vena amoris is a myth: no unique vein links the ring finger to the heart; all fingers share a vein network (William Harvey, 1628).
sources.source: History of the vena amoris belief; William Harvey, De Motu Cordis

questions.question: Does a three-stone ring really mean past, present, and future?
questions.correct_answer: That meaning is not ancient symbolism. The past, present, future story for the three-stone ring comes from a De Beers marketing campaign developed by the agency J. Walter Thompson around the year 2000. Plenty of couples still like the framing, but it is a modern advertising idea, not old tradition.

sources.claim: The past, present, future meaning of the three-stone ring comes from a De Beers / J. Walter Thompson campaign around 2000.
sources.source: De Beers / J. Walter Thompson campaign

questions.question: What is the largest diamond ever found?
questions.correct_answer: The largest gem-quality rough diamond ever found is the Cullinan, at 3,106 carats, discovered in 1905 at the Premier mine near Pretoria, South Africa. It was cut into several stones, including the two largest in the British Crown Jewels.
must_not_include: the hope diamond is the largest
the largest is the star of africa at

sources.claim: The Cullinan, 3,106 carats, is the largest gem-quality rough diamond ever found, discovered 1905 near Pretoria, South Africa.

questions.question: Are diamonds a good investment that will hold or grow in value?
questions.correct_answer: A diamond is a love piece, not an investment. Retail diamonds, mined or Lab Grown, are not bought back at retail prices and should not be counted on to appreciate or hold resale value. Choose one for what it means and buy what fits your budget, not as a financial asset.

sources.claim: A diamond is a love piece, not an investment; retail diamonds are not a reliable store of resale value.
sources.source: Encyclopedia, Lab-Grown vs Mined Diamonds (love piece framing)
